name: Grace Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out the door at quarter to seven to catch the 7:05 bus up Station Road. First call is Mr Doyle, who had a stroke last year, so I get him up, washed, dressed and give him his porridge and his tablets. Then it's about eight more calls before lunch, most of them fifteen or thirty minutes, and I walk between the ones the bus doesn't reach. The agency doesn't pay for the walking, which still makes me angry every single week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. Mrs Abara has dementia and some days she thinks I'm her niece, and I just go along with it because it makes her happy. What wears me out is the clock, because fifteen minutes isn't enough to do a wash and have a proper chat. And the money, honestly. I'm on a zero-hours contract, so if a client goes into hospital, my hours just vanish that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone then. Care is people work and it always will be. I'd probably share something on the union page saying the real problem was never robots, it's that we're paid like we don't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now. Joel (my partner) works nights at the warehouse and between us we just about cover the rent on the flat above the launderette. Nothing about AI being hype fixes the fact that I've got less than a month's money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and keep going to the union meetings at the community centre on the first Tuesday of the month. I keep saying I'll finish my care certificate, the module I failed on medication, so I'd try that again in the spring. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff because I never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of relieved, but not happy. Relieved that nobody's coming for my job, but I'm still lying awake about the gas bill. A world where AI is just hype still leaves me walking between houses in the rain for no pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hours vanish when a client goes into hospital. What happened the last time that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Doyle went into hospital in March for nearly three weeks. I lost about eleven hours a week and nobody at the agency offered me anything else. I had to borrow forty pounds from Joel's mum for the electric, and I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the way things are now, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency owners, first, because they take the council money and squeeze us. And the government, for paying the council so little that fifteen-minute visits seem normal. Nobody in charge has ever tried to wash an old man and make him laugh in fifteen minutes.

say: I'd tell everyone care is **people work** and always will be.
I'd post that the real problem was never robots but **low pay** for carers.
think: My life stays **as hard** as it is now, with less than a month saved.
Hype or not, nothing fixes **zero-hours** contracts and unpaid walking time.
do: Keep doing my **morning rounds** and go to the union meeting every month.
Retake the **medication module** I failed on my care certificate in spring.
Stay away from **AI tools**, the same as I always have.
feel: **Relieved** nobody is coming for my job, but still awake at night over **bills**.
S0.quote: Nobody in charge has ever tried to wash an old man and make him laugh in fifteen minutes.
fieldNote: Grace already lives one hospital admission away from **losing hours**; AI adds nothing to that worry here.
Her anger targets **agency owners** and council funding, not technology.
She borrowed **forty pounds** in March and still feels the shame of asking.

steps.text: Keep the morning round starting with Mr Doyle at 7:30
Go to the union meeting at the community centre each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can have the paperwork, but they can't have the person in the bed. At work I'd be the one moaning in the group chat that the office is spending money on software instead of on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. The bits AI takes are the bits the office does: the rota, the call checks, the care notes. That means whoever runs the computer gets to decide how long I spend in each house, and they'll always decide on less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a say on any new system before it comes in. I'd cut back now, maybe stop the phone contract and go pay-as-you-go, because I can see shorter visits meaning fewer paid minutes. I'd keep doing the job, because I don't know anything else and there's nothing else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Like there's one more thing watching me. The agency app already beeps when I'm two minutes late at my client's house, and I'm not letting a computer make that beep louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the app the agency uses. What does it do now, and what would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I tap in when I arrive and tap out when I leave, and the office can see if I'm late. If AI planned the rota, it'd squeeze the gaps between houses even tighter and nobody would hear me say the bus doesn't come that often. Simone in the office at least listens, even if she can't do much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a colleague started using the AI tools and you didn't, how would that go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably. Kerry, who started the same month as me, uses her phone for everything, and she'd fly through the notes. I'd be slower and the office would notice, and I'd probably get the worst calls on the rota.

say: I'd say AI can take the **paperwork** but never the person in the bed.
I'd complain in the **group chat** that money goes on software, not carers.
think: AI takes the **office jobs**: the rota, the call checks and the care notes.
Whoever runs the computer will decide on **less time** in each house.
do: Push the **union** to get a say before any new system comes in.
Switch my phone to **pay-as-you-go** to cut costs this year.
Keep doing the **rounds**, because there's nothing else nearby.
feel: **Tired** and watched, like there's one more thing timing her visits.
S1.quote: The agency app already beeps when I'm two minutes late at my client's house, and I'm not letting a computer make that beep louder.
fieldNote: Grace sees Steady Disruption as the office getting **sharper tools** to cut her minutes.
She fears falling behind **Kerry**, a colleague who uses her phone for everything.
Her refusal to use AI could cost her the **better calls** on the rota.

steps.text: Ask the union to demand a say on new rota software
Switch the phone contract to pay-as-you-go to save money
Keep doing the same eight calls a morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly, in every place I could. I'd say you don't hand your nan to a machine, and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it means I'm finished by the time I'm thirty-one. In 2028 the office goes to AI straight away, so the rotas and the checks get worse overnight. Then three years later the hands-on bit goes too, and that's all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every union campaign and march and write to our MP about keeping people in care. I'd cut everything I could, no takeaways, no nights out, and try to put twenty pounds a week by, though I don't know how. If the robots came in 2031, I'd probably end up leaning on Joel's mum or on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, picturing it. I keep thinking of Mrs Abara being turned over by a machine that doesn't know she likes her pillow on the left. I left school at sixteen, and caring is the one thing I found I'm good at. Robots taking it at thirty-one would leave me with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Between 2028 and 2031, before the robots come, what does your working week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably worse than now, because the AI would be running the rota and squeezing every minute out of us. There might be more work for a bit because the agency would be cutting office staff and moving everything onto us carers. But I'd know the clock was ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joel the night you heard robots were coming in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joel we need to stop pretending the warehouse is safe too, because robots would come for his job at the same time. I'd probably cry, to be honest. Then I'd make him a cup of tea and we'd work out what we could sell.

say: I'd say you don't hand your **nan** to a machine.
I'd sign every **petition** and shout about it everywhere I could.
think: I'd be **finished** by thirty-one, once robots take the hands-on work in 2031.
From 2028 the **AI rota** would make every visit tighter overnight.
do: Join **union campaigns** and write to our MP about keeping people in care.
Cut takeaways and nights out and try to save **twenty pounds** a week.
Lean on **Joel's mum** or benefits if the robots arrive in 2031.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of a machine turning Mrs Abara over.
**Scared** that the one thing she's good at would be gone.
S2.quote: I left school at sixteen, and caring is the one thing I found I'm good at. Robots taking it at thirty-one would leave me with nothing.
fieldNote: Grace sees the **three-year gap** as a slow countdown, not breathing room.
Her partner's **warehouse job** is exposed too, so the whole household is at risk.
She jumps straight to **political action**, but has no personal plan beyond cutting back.

steps.text: March and petition with the union against robots in home care
Write to the local MP about keeping people in care
Drop takeaways and nights out to save twenty pounds a week
Ask Joel's mum for help if work stops in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd say carers need to get together now, while there's still time to fight for rules on robots in people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'd have a bit longer, but I'd still be out by thirty-four or thirty-five. I don't have the money to train for something else, and I didn't finish school. Five years just means a longer time to dread it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly involved in the union, maybe become the rep for our agency if nobody else wants it. I'd try to put a bit by every month, even if it's only fifteen pounds. And I'd wait and see what the robots actually look like before I panic about changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more heavy, if that makes sense. Like a cloud that's always there. Five years' warning means a longer time to dread the robots, not more money to escape them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years instead of two change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the union time to push for a law that says a person has to be there, I suppose. That's the bit that gives me some hope. But it doesn't give me savings, and that's what you need to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. Would you still say that with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to use some of it, if the agency made us. I'd hate it, but I'd do what I was told. I just wouldn't trust it, and I'd still be doing my notes the way I always have in my head first.

say: I'd say carers should **organise now** while there's still time.
I'd call for **rules on robots** in people's homes.
think: I'd still be **out by thirty-five**, just a bit later.
Five years doesn't give me the **savings** I'd need to retrain.
do: Volunteer as **union rep** for my agency if nobody else will.
Save **fifteen pounds** a month, even if it's tight.
Wait to see the **robots** before deciding about another job.
feel: Less sick but **heavy**, like a cloud that's always there.
S3.quote: Five years' warning means a longer time to dread the robots, not more money to escape them.
fieldNote: Grace pins her hope on a **law** requiring a person in the room.
She'd use AI only **under orders** and still wouldn't trust it.
More time makes her more **organised**, but not less exposed.

steps.text: Volunteer as the union rep for Brightpath Homecare
Save fifteen pounds a month in a jar
Watch how the first care robots work before looking elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to plan properly, so they'd better. I'd tell people at the union that we should be fighting for retraining money, not just against robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels far enough away that I'd probably ignore it for a while. That's the problem with me, I don't do anything until it's on top of me. But I'd be about forty when the robots come, and that's young enough to be stuck for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in care, keep going to the union and maybe finally finish my care certificate. I'd try to save a little each month for when it comes. If there was free training through the union, I might do something, but I'd have to see it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but it's still there. Ten years sounds like ages until I remember I'll be forty with no savings and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about forty when the robots arrive. What would you want to be doing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still caring, honestly, but maybe as a senior carer who checks on the robots and the clients. I'd want to be the person families trust. But I don't know if that job would even exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this ten-year picture that you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the lifting. My back's already sore and I'm only twenty-seven. If a machine helped get Mr Doyle out of bed without hurting either of us, I wouldn't mind that, as long as I was still there.

say: I'd say ten years gives the **government** time to plan properly.
I'd push the union to fight for **retraining money** too.
think: Ten years feels far enough away that I'd **ignore it** for a while.
I'd be **forty** with no savings and no other trade when robots come.
do: Stay in care and finally finish my **care certificate**.
Put a little into **savings** each month for when it arrives.
Look at free **union training** if it's actually offered.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, but the worry is still there.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like ages until I remember I'll be forty with no savings and no other trade.
fieldNote: Grace admits she **puts off** acting until problems are on top of her.
She'd welcome **lifting help** for her sore back if she stays in the room.
Her hope is to become the carer **families trust**, though she doubts that role will exist.

steps.text: Finish the care certificate, including the medication module
Put a small amount into savings every month
Push the union to win retraining money for carers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time and no money and Joel's warehouse goes too. What would help is a proper wage now, so we'd have something saved, and a law saying a real person has to be in the room with old people. My clients don't need a faster machine. My clients need someone who remembers how they take their tea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the families. Half the families I see would be glad of a cheaper robot, because they can't afford us either. That's what nobody wants to say.

headlineQuote: My clients don't need a faster machine. My clients need someone who remembers how they take their tea.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** carer on a zero-hours contract, walking between houses in a small market town.
She lives with **Joel**, who works nights in a warehouse, and has under a month saved.
She never uses **AI tools** and blames agency owners and council cuts for her low pay.
She grows from anxious to **alarmed** under fast AGI, then settles back to anxious with ten years.
Her answer is always the **union** and a law keeping a person in the room.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time, no money, and Joel's warehouse job goes too.
whatWouldHelp: A **proper wage** now so she could save something.
A **law** saying a real person must be in the room with older people.
